title: Listening to the Original Dixieland Jazz Band and the All Star Trio
summary: He played along with ODJB records, copying saxophonist Benny Krueger, and copied Wheeler Wadsworth's C-melody solo on Just Blue.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Had you been listening to the music of the day, what were --
What were the things that you liked.

Well, at that time, there was Whiteman at that time, but there was a lot of -- the Original Dixieland Jazz Band. I listened to a lot of that. Joseph C. Smith. "There Are Smiles That Make You Happy." No saxophone, he just had strings in his orchestra and I think he played in the Waldorf.
I guess the Original Dixieland Jazz Band was 1917.
Right. This was about roughly 1919. Let's see, late 1919 I suppose. I graduated from high school in '21 and I had this when I was about a junior.

And I listened to them and I used to like the band, of course. Who didn't. But the way they did things, they played things like "Margie" and "Strut Miss Lizzie." You know, they used to play -- they'd take a pop tune and put a tune like "Strut Miss Lizzie" or "Sweet Mama, Poppa's Getting Mad" in the middle of it and go back to the tunes they would play and I used to play along with them.
Right. Put the record on and play along with it, and they had -- well, they had two or three different saxophone players but the one who lasted with them
was Benny Gruger, if you remember and I used to try to play everything that he played.

I used to listen to the All Star Trio, Wheeler Wadsworth. Wheeler Wadsworth and one of the guys I used to play with later, he was a drummer and he played xylophones. When I worked later with Nat Shilkret and -- Green, Joe Green.

They didn't have a drummer, they just had a piano. I think it was maybe Frankie Bennett, somebody like that. Frankie Bennett and maybe Joe Green or one of the Greens. George Hamilton Green and Wheeler Wadsworth, and they used to play one that I copied, that is, no music. By ear. "Just Blue." It was a fantastic C-melody saxophone which the guy played, which Wadsworth played.

That's right. It was "Just Blue" and it had a lot of the blue feeling, yes. But it got all over the instrument. He exploited the instrument from the low register to the high register and that interested me. I later played it as a solo in high school along with some other tune like "Ave Maria" or something like that.
